lead: Clustering creates groups without labels. To know if the groups are meaningful we need evaluation measures. Internal measures look at the data itself, external measures compare to a known class label. They help choose the number of clusters K and check stability. Only a few universities teach these advanced validation techniques.
prereq: You need: Unsupervised learning basics, K‑means, and basic linear algebra.

blocks.text: Silhouette measures how well a point fits its own cluster compared to the nearest other cluster. For a point i, a(i) is the average distance to all other points in the same cluster. b(i) is the average distance to points in the nearest different cluster. The silhouette s(i) = (b(i)‑a(i)) ÷ max(a(i),b(i)). The value lies between –1 and 1. A high positive value means the point is well placed.

blocks.where: s(i) is silhouette of point i; a(i) is intra‑cluster average distance; b(i) is nearest‑cluster average distance.

blocks.text: Davies‑Bouldin (DB) uses the ratio of intra‑cluster scatter to inter‑cluster separation. For each cluster i, compute S_i = average distance of points in i to its centroid. Compute M_ij = distance between centroids of i and j. DB = (1/K) Σ_i max_{j≠i} (S_i + S_j) ÷ M_ij. Lower DB means better clustering.

blocks.where: K is number of clusters; S_i is scatter of cluster i; M_ij is centroid distance between i and j.

items: Silhouette is easy to compute for any distance metric.
DB works with numeric features and can use any distance metric; Euclidean distance is the most common choice.
Both indices assume compact, spherical clusters.

blocks.text: When true class labels are available, external indices compare the clustering to the ground truth.

items: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) counts pairs of points that are placed together or apart in both the clustering and the true labeling, corrected for chance. ARI ranges from –1 to 1; 1 means perfect agreement.
Purity assigns each cluster to the most frequent true class in it and measures the fraction of correctly assigned points. Purity is between 0 and 1. It ignores the number of clusters.
Normalised Mutual Information (NMI) measures shared information between the clustering and the true labeling, normalised by the average entropy. NMI also ranges from 0 to 1.

blocks.where: RI is Rand Index; Expected_RI is its expected value for random labeling; Max_RI = 1.
I(C;K) is mutual information between true classes C and clusters K; H(.) is entropy.

blocks.text: The elbow method plots an internal index versus K. The point where improvement slows is the elbow. For silhouette, the peak often indicates the best K.

items: Run the clustering algorithm for K = 2 up to a chosen maximum K (for example, 10).
Compute the average silhouette for each K.
Plot K on the x‑axis and silhouette on the y‑axis.
Select K at the highest silhouette or where the curve flattens.

blocks.text: Stability tests use resampling. Split the data, cluster each subset, and compare the two clusterings with ARI or NMI. High agreement means the result is robust to data variation.

items: Do not rely on a single index; combine silhouette with DB or external scores.
For high‑dimensional data, reduce dimensions first (e.g., PCA) before computing distances.

examples.question: Six points are clustered into two groups: {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}. Their coordinates are A(0,0), B(1,0), C(0,1), D(5,5), E(6,5), F(5,6). Compute the average Silhouette score using Euclidean distance.
steps: For each point, calculate a(i) = average distance to points in the same cluster.
For each point, calculate b(i) = average distance to points in the other cluster.
Average s(i) over all six points.

traps: Using Euclidean distance for Silhouette when the data are categorical leads to meaningless scores.
Confusing a(i) (intra‑cluster) with b(i) (nearest‑cluster) and swapping them in the formula gives negative values.
Choosing K solely from the highest silhouette without checking DB or stability can over‑fit noisy data.

quiz.q: What is the range of the Silhouette score?
Explain why a lower Davies‑Bouldin index indicates better clustering.
quiz.a: DB is the average of worst‑case cluster similarity; smaller similarity means clusters are compact and well separated.

quiz.q: A clustering of 100 points yields an average Silhouette of 0.42. If you increase K and the Silhouette rises to 0.55, what does this suggest?
quiz.a: Increasing K improved the separation of points; the new K is likely closer to the true number of groups.

quiz.q: Given true class labels, a clustering obtains ARI = 0.73. Is this clustering good? Justify.
quiz.a: ARI near 1 means strong agreement; 0.73 indicates a good but not perfect match.

quiz.q: Two clusterings of the same data have Silhouette scores 0.48 and 0.48 but DB scores 0.65 and 0.45 respectively. Which clustering is preferable and why?
quiz.a: Both have equal silhouette, but the lower DB (0.45) shows better inter‑cluster separation, so the second clustering is preferable.

quiz.q: During stability testing, two resampled runs give NMI = 0.92. What does this imply about the clustering algorithm?
quiz.a: High NMI indicates the algorithm produces consistent clusterings across different samples, showing robustness.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, clustering validation is used for customer segmentation, fraud detection, and recommendation systems where business impact matters more than a single index. Research explores validation for high‑dimensional and graph data, often using deep clustering methods. Emerging curricula combine validation with explainable AI to justify cluster decisions. Look for recent surveys on cluster evaluation and for toolkits such as scikit‑learn's metrics module.
